name: Lip plumping device
lead: A lip plumping device is a small cup or suction tool placed over the lips to draw blood and fluid into the tissue and produce temporary swelling. Some versions add vibration or warmth. It is promoted as a do-it-yourself alternative to lip filler that gives a fuller look for a short time. Wikipedia lists suction pumps among the non-surgical alternatives to lip augmentation, describing them as devices that use vacuum to raise pressure in the lips and cause temporary swelling.[1]

No peer-reviewed clinical study of suction lip-plumping devices has been identified. Published research on lip plumping concerns topical plumper products, which act by irritation or vasodilation, and injectable fillers. Trials of topical plumpers have found short-lived increases in lip fullness lasting from minutes to a few hours, and case reports describe contact urticaria.[2][3][4]
Reported risks of excessive suction include bruising, broken capillaries, pain and swelling; the effect is described as fading within hours.

paras: Suction lip plumpers are small silicone or plastic cups, sometimes shaped like a lip, that the user presses over the mouth while squeezing or using a pump or battery to create negative pressure. Electric versions add heat or vibration. They are sold online and through beauty retailers.

Negative pressure pulls blood and tissue fluid into the lips, causing engorgement and mild swelling. No new tissue forms, and the swelling subsides as circulation normalizes. Topical plumpers work differently: Wikipedia describes them as products that irritate the lip skin with ingredients such as capsaicin so that the lips swell temporarily.[1]
No studies found of suction lip-plumping devices.

A single-site open-label trial of a topical plumping product enrolled 22 subjects, 18 of whom completed it. Clinicians judged lip fullness improved in all 18 at 15 minutes and in 12 (67 percent) at one hour, with the benefit declining after that.[2]

A randomized study of a ginger-based plumper in 60 women found that vascularization of the lip increased in the first 15 minutes and then declined. Volume increases were detected by 3D profilometry (about 0.5 mm in lip protrusion) but not by anthropometric measures, and the authors concluded that the product temporarily enhances vasodilation and lip volume.[3]
A 2009 case report described contact urticaria to a lip plumper in a young boy.[4]

A 2025 prospective safety study evaluated hyaluronic acid fillers for lip enhancement and perioral correction.[5] Fillers are injected treatments with different effects and risks, which Wikipedia describes as including swelling, bruising, lumpiness and allergic reaction.[1]
A 2025 study in Proceedings of the Royal Society B examined how manipulating lip size alters perceived facial attractiveness.[6]

Wikipedia notes that swelling and bruising are common after lip augmentation procedures in general.[1] For suction devices, the commonly reported risks are bruising, small broken blood vessels, pain and swelling after overly strong or prolonged suction; no studies have quantified them. Reviews of lip-care cosmetics describe contact urticaria and allergic contact dermatitis from product ingredients.[7]
Suction plumpers are discussed as an inexpensive, no-needle alternative to filler, often used before photographs. Proponents describe the effect as noticeable but brief.
